did_you_know.text: Scholars connect Yavan with the Ionians and Greeks, and Madai with the ancient Medes east of Mesopotamia. These names reflect peoples and regions known in the ancient world.
The Hebrew word for “islands” can refer not only to islands, but also to distant lands across the sea.

The name Nimrod resembles the Hebrew root meaning “to rebel,” so Jewish tradition sometimes connects it with rebellion. This is a linguistic interpretation, not a proven historical explanation of the name.
Shinar is usually understood as a biblical name for southern Mesopotamia, the region between the Euphrates and Tigris Rivers. Babel is generally identified with the city of Babylon in modern Iraq.
Nineveh stood on the Tigris River and later became the capital of the Assyrian Empire. Its ruins lie near the modern Iraqi city of Mosul.
Nineveh was an exceptionally large city, but “the great city” may also refer to the wider urban area around it. In the ancient world, cities often included nearby farmland and villages.
Sidon was an important Phoenician port on the Lebanese coast. It appears often in the Bible and other ancient sources and was a center of trade and seafaring.
The word “Hebrew” may be linguistically connected with the name Eber, although scholars debate whether this is truly its origin. In this way, the biblical family tree links peoples with their names.
The name Peleg is related in Hebrew to the root meaning “to divide” or “to split.” Such wordplay between a person’s name and its meaning is common in biblical narratives.
Many of the names in Joktan’s list are associated by scholars with regions in southern Arabia. Their exact locations remain uncertain because some of the names later disappeared from use.

Scholars often call this chapter the “Table of Nations” because it presents the world’s peoples through families, lands, and languages. It is an ancient way of explaining relationships among peoples, not a modern population census.
